name: Polished
process: Honing is carried on through finer grits and finished with a polishing powder or an oxalic-acid compound, which leaves the face glossy. Travertine's voids are filled before polishing: for one Spanish travertine, a beige gypsum-based plaster in the large pores, then an epoxy-silicone resin dressing, then the polish.
processSources: Dynamic Stone Tools (trade guide, undated), 'Grit progression by stone type: polishing sequences guide', https://dynamicstonetools.com/blogs/news/grit-progression-by-stone-type-polishing-sequences-guide

abrasiveSequence.conditions: the full polish sequence for marble, then polishing powder or an oxalic-acid compound; trade practice; the grit scale is not named

definition.text: Polished: a glossy surface which brings out the full colour and character of the stone.
definition.source: Natural Stone Institute (2022) Dimension Stone Design Manual, chapter 12 'Travertine' (Specification, Product Description, Technical Data), pp. 12-1 to 12-14, https://transparencycatalog.com/assets/uploads/greener-images/12-TRAVERTINE-2022.pdf, Product Description 4.1.1

gloss.source: McDonell J.A., Kyle R.C. (Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing Co.) (1994) US Patent 5,282,900 'Nonwoven surface treating articles, system including same, and method of treating calcium carbonate-containing surfaces with said system', https://patents.google.com/patent/US5282900A/en
gloss.conditions: 60 degree geometry; the patent calls a marble surface of about 75 or more 'high gloss'

glossTrade.source: Kuhn T., Rose Restoration (trade guide, 2026-03-25), 'The GC Guide to Specifying Stone Restoration in Commercial Bids'; gloss geometry not stated, https://www.roserestoration.com/blog/gc-guide-specifying-stone-restoration-commercial-bids/
glossTrade.conditions: 'high-gloss polish'; geometry not stated; a satin finish is 40-50

openPorosity.source: Urosevic M., Sebastian-Pardo E., Cardell C. (2010) 'Rough and polished travertine building stone decay evaluated by a marine aerosol ageing test', Construction and Building Materials 24:1438-1448 (Olivillo travertine, Alhama de Almeria, Spain, sawn vein-cut), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2010.01.011, Table 3
openPorosity.conditions: mercury-intrusion open porosity after filling and polishing (8.16 % before): the resin closes the near-surface pores

colour.text: Filling and polishing darkened and warmed a travertine: L* 69.78 to 62.00, a* 1.83 to 5.52, b* 7.31 to 15.69, measured with a Minolta CR-210 at 0 degree viewing.
colour.source: Urosevic M., Sebastian-Pardo E., Cardell C. (2010) 'Rough and polished travertine building stone decay evaluated by a marine aerosol ageing test', Construction and Building Materials 24:1438-1448 (Olivillo travertine, Alhama de Almeria, Spain, sawn vein-cut), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2010.01.011, Table 5
colour.note: the rows are in Substances/travertine.json, optics.measuredColour

physics.text: Polishing does not change the stone's index or its F0. It removes the roughness that scattered white light from the first surface, so the reflection gathers into a sharp lobe and the body colour shows undiluted.
physics.source: Urosevic M., Sebastian-Pardo E., Cardell C. (2010) 'Rough and polished travertine building stone decay evaluated by a marine aerosol ageing test', Construction and Building Materials 24:1438-1448 (Olivillo travertine, Alhama de Almeria, Spain, sawn vein-cut), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2010.01.011, Table 5 ; Ghosh G. (1999) 'Dispersion-equation coefficients for the refractive index and birefringence of calcite and quartz crystals', Optics Communications 163:95-102; coefficients as tabulated at https://refractiveindex.info/?shelf=main&book=CaCO3&page=Ghosh-o and https://refractiveindex.info/?shelf=main&book=CaCO3&page=Ghosh-e
physics.derivation: from the measured colour change and the calcite F0 (Substances/travertine.json, optics.specularF0)

photograph: Sharp mirror images of doorways, lamps and people, softened only a little.
The stone darker and warmer in colour than its honed neighbour.
Resin-filled voids glossier than the stone around them; cement-filled voids duller.
Where people walk, lanes of lost gloss (see stone.foot-traffic-wear).

unverified.reason: No measured BRDF of polished travertine or Crema Marfil was found; a renderer's roughness must be fitted to a specimen or a measured polished marble.
A search summary cites mean values of 18 to 24 for polished limestones (Coskun, Sariisik and Sariisik 2016, Cogent Engineering 3:1217821); not read at the source.
